As of 310 AM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain chances increase Saturday night into Sunday as 
the remnants of Hurricane Isaias move farther inland. There is a
Slight Risk (level 2/5) for severe weather Sunday. 

Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the FL panhandle late last evening 
and was just starting to cross into Alabama as of 2am as it 
degrades. Here locally in the Mid-Atlantic sfc high pressure is 
still in charge for now. Isaias will transition into an extra-
tropical system as it treks north today toward TN/KY/WV. A warm 
front will extend east from the parent low and push north towards 
the FA. A subtle coastal trough forming along the front along with 
high pressure ridging down the mountains will set up a relatively 
weak CAD over the piedmont tonight into tomorrow. The FA will spend 
Sunday morning-mid day in the warm sector, then the low will 
progress northeast and drag a cold front through Sunday evening. The 
evolution of this system will bring widespread rain to the area as 
well as the chance for a few tornadoes and strong winds. 

Rain will arrive ahead of the warm front as early as this afternoon 
to far southern/southwestern counties then spreads across the area 
in earnest after 8pm, continuing overnight. This is when the bulk 
of appreciable rainfall should fall and when the aforementioned 
coastal trough could locally enhance rainfall near the Outer Banks. 
The 00z high res models and ensembles as well as the global 
deterministic models are leaning hard on the idea of a dry slot 
across central portions of the area, roughly along the I-95 
corridor, after the warm front lifts through the area. A secondary 
line of showers/storms would then impact the area ahead of the cold 
front. As a result, the projected precip totals are less than 
previous model suites. The high res models indicate a widespread 
~0.5" with locally higher 1-2" along coastal SE VA and NE NC. 
Meanwhile, a global ensemble like the GEFS has something similar in 
its 10th percentile with a mean of 1-2" for most and 2-2.5" for the 
southeast. The 90th percentile has around 3". The NBM, of course, 
reflects this spread with a wide range in its percentiles from less 
than an inch in the 10th to around 3" in the 90th. The dry slot was 
incorporated into the QPF since confidence is increasing in this 
solution. Now expecting 1-1.5" total along the coast and across the 
piedmont with central portions of the area receiving less than an 
inch. Areas near the Albemarle Sound may experience locally higher 
amounts of 2-3". Flood threat is low, but urban and poor drainage 
areas could see localized flooding Sunday morning. 

The threat for severe weather comes in as the low traverses northern 
VA/MD and drags a cold front through the local area. Most of the 
CAMs depict a broken line of convection and/or supercells Sunday 
afternoon ahead of the front. An influx of instability to around 800-
1000 J/kg (per RRFS/REFS) would support strong to severe storms. The 
modeled wind profile is favorable for supercells with SE winds at 
the sfc, strengthening deep layer shear, and curved hodographs. This 
could mean strong to severe winds and even a few tornadoes. Of 
course if the dry slot is never realized, it would likely put a 
damper on instability and therefore severe chances. Also, the CAD 
setup will likely limit severe potential for at least areas NW of 
Richmond. SPC has upgraded the entire FA to a Slight Risk with a 5% 
tornado risk and 15% severe wind risk. 

Regarding temperatures, highs will be in the upper 60s in the 
piedmont and low 70s E of I-95 today. Tomorrow, highs will range 
from the upper 70s/around 80 in the southeast to the low 70s in the 
northwest. Breezy conditions are forecast as well with gusts of 20-
25mph inland and 25-35mph at the coast starting this afternoon 
through tomorrow, peaking early Sunday morning. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...A brief warmup is expected early next week with 
cooler temperatures later in the week.

Aloft, a ridge centered across the central CONUS gradually builds 
into the region through the week. Meanwhile, surface high pressure 
remains centered across the Deep South through midweek before a 
second area of high pressure builds in from the north late in the 
week. This will result in a brief warm-up with highs in the mid to 
upper 70s on Monday and low 80s on Tues. Per usual, the Eastern 
Shore can expect to be several degrees cooler each day. Still a tad 
warm on Wed, then cooling back to seasonal norms later in the week 
through the weekend. Mostly dry through mid-week, then trending 
toward a more unsettled pattern starting Thurs. 

KEY MESSAGE 3..Nuisance to Minor tidal flooding is expected with
the high tide cycle Sunday for portions of Hampton Roads, the western
shore of the Chesapeake Bay and the lower Maryland eastern shore.
